A Sugarcoated Collapse

By: Anina Peens | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Along the north coast of KwaZulu-Natal, sugar built an empire over the past 130 years but now, its future no longer looks so sweet.

Unique Selling Point:
This story captures the human cost of industrial collapse, following families whose lives span generations of sugar production, from indentured labour to modern land reform beneficiaries, now facing an uncertain future.

Summary:
This is one of South Africa’s most important and underreported historical and economic stories, one that many younger generations may barely know.
It began in 1860, when ships carrying indentured Indian labourers arrived on the shores of Durban to build what would become one of the country’s most influential agricultural industries. Over the decades, the sugar industry grew into a vast economic empire, shaping communities, sustaining generations of families, and controlling some of the most valuable land in South Africa. Entire towns were built around its mills, and its influence defined the development of KwaZulu-Natal’s north coast. Now, more than a century later, that empire faces an uncertain future, as corporate collapse, global competition, and a government widely criticised for failing to protect local industry, threaten to dismantle one of the country’s oldest economic foundations.


Further information:
Tongaat Hulett is facing an almost certain liquidation. Its collapse threatens not only an industry, but entire towns, communities, and a history stretching back more than a century.
Founded in 1892, Tongaat Hulett played a central role in the development of Durban’s north coast and the rise of the Indian middle class in KwaZulu-Natal. The company owns vast tracts of agricultural land, some of the most valuable in the country on the North Coast corridor between Ballito and Durban. It is this land that now sits at the centre of a growing dispute, leaving the future of hundreds of thousands of people uncertain.
The company’s decline began in 2019, when it emerged that Tongaat Hulett had overstated its financial position by nearly R4 billion. It would become one of the biggest corporate scandals in South Africa since Steinhoff, yet received relatively little public scrutiny. Once listed on both the Johannesburg and London Stock Exchanges, the company was subsequently delisted from both, as investor confidence collapsed and banks withdrew their support.
Crippled by debt, Tongaat Hulett entered business rescue in 2022. A Zimbabwean consortium, Vision Sugar, stepped in with the intention of rescuing the company. But disagreements between investors, creditors, and shareholders have stalled those efforts. Now, Tongaat Hulett is expected to file for liquidation on 24 February. Its bank accounts have already been frozen, and salaries will only be paid until the end of March. Beyond that, the future of its mills and the communities that depend on them, remains uncertain.
The closure of a sugar mill is rarely temporary. Once shut down, the surrounding economic ecosystem begins to unravel. Farmers lose access to processing facilities. Workers lose employment. Local businesses collapse. Entire towns begin to decline.
At the heart of the dispute is Tongaat Hulett’s land portfolio. Currently zoned for agriculture, parts of this land are valued at approximately R20,000 per hectare. But if rezoned for residential or industrial development, its value could increase exponentially, reaching as much as R10 million per hectare. With liquidation looming, this land will be sold to repay creditors. The fear among many is that it could ultimately fall into foreign hands, transforming one of South Africa’s most historically significant agricultural corridors into a development battleground.
At the same time, the broader sugar industry is under mounting pressure from imported sugar. Cheap sugar from countries such as Brazil, India, and Thailand has flooded the South African market, increasing dramatically over the past year. Local farmers now find themselves unable to compete. Sugar is stockpiling in warehouses, unsold and unprocessed, while mills struggle to remain operational.
The industry supports an intricate ecosystem that includes more than 20,000 small-scale farmers, many of whom are land reform beneficiaries. For these farmers, sugar is not just a crop, it is their only source of income. The collapse of Tongaat Hulett would trigger widespread unemployment, accelerate rural decline, and drive migration into already overcrowded cities. In KwaZulu-Natal, where economic instability has historically contributed to social unrest, the consequences could be severe.
Tongaat Hulett’s history is deeply intertwined with South Africa’s past. From the 1860s, Indian labourers were brought to work on the sugar plantations. Many were housed in barracks built by the company. Sunrise Barracks remains one of the oldest surviving examples. Today, descendants of those original labourers still live there, their lives spanning generations of work in the sugar fields and mills.
That history now stands on the edge of disappearance. There are growing concerns that the barracks may be demolished as part of future land redevelopment. What took generations to build could vanish within years.
Entire towns, including Empangeni, Amatikulu, Mount Edgecombe, Maidstone, and communities as far as Pongola owe their existence to the sugar industry. The north coast itself was shaped by sugar. While development will inevitably continue, the question remains what will happen to the people whose lives, livelihoods, and identities are rooted in this land.
The land will endure. The economy will move forward. But for those who built their lives around sugar, the future has never been more uncertain.

I N V E S T I G A T I O N 
Sugar-coated Collapse
For more than a century, sugar built an empire along the north coast of KwaZulu Natal, shaping communities and controlling valuable land. Now, global competition and the collapse of a corporate giant threaten its future. As cheap imports replace local product and liquidation looms, farmers face the loss of an existence that’s been in their families for generations. Over a million livelihoods and decades of history hover on the brink as the industry faces a bitter reckoning.
Producer: Anina Peens | Presenter: Claire Mawisa


Script:


SUGARCOATED COLLAPSE final for mnet
(Keval Bodasing) Our story begins with my forefather, Babu Bodasing. He was born in Agra, Northern India and as we all know, Indians arrived in South Africa, in 1860.He boarded a ship on the first of August 1874. It was a month-long journey from Calcutta down to what was then Port Natal. And her arrived in South Africa, first of September 1874. He served his indentureship which was 5 years for the Glasgow natal sugar company where he was elevated to working at the sugar mill.
(Claire Mawisa) Sugar cane was introduced in South Africa during British colonial rule in the 1800s. Thousands of workers were brought from India under indentureship, paid labour often likened to slavery. Conditions were harsh, with contracts binding workers to plantations for five to seven years. But after his contract finished, Keval Bodasing’s great, great grandfather chose to stay.
(Keval Bodasing) He were given the option of a return passage back to India, or you could exchange that for a monetary value and he was able to use these proceeds to purchase 6 acres of land. By 1910 he had purchased this farm, which is known as Hydepark. He passed away in 1919 and at that time he had owned 8000 acres of land
(Claire Mawisa) Wow
(Keval Bodasing) And he became the largest landowner out of any of the Indentured labourers at the time.
(Claire Mawisa) Was it always a desire as well for you to continue the legacy that is so rich?
(Keval Bodasing) It was engrained in me from birth that I would one day continue the farming legacy that we have. And ah, so, I kind of knew this was my destiny no matter what happened.
(Claire Mawisa) Vast stretches of sugarcane dominate the KwaZulu Natal coast. It’s been the lifeforce of the economy here for over a century. At the epicentre of what’s known as the sugar belt is the historic town of Tongaat. It’s the site of the Maidstone Mill, where the country’s first cane was processed in 1903. It was a vibrant and promising time. Companies like Tongaat Hulett gave farmers security, building an entire economy around the crop.
(Keval Bodasing) One has to look at the canegrowers and the millers and how they are intertwined. Neither can exist without each other and the growers require milling capacity in order to sustain their business. This map is over a hundred years old
(Claire Mawisa) The business model remained largely unchanged. Cane is still cut by hand, and generational growers like the Bodasings have generally delivered to the same mills.
(Keval Bodasing) The N2 didn’t exist its currently on this alignment here.
(Thomas Funke) As sugarcane is harvested, it has to be processed within 48 to 72 hours otherwise it deteriorates, and the farmers get penalised for sending poor quality cane to the sugar mill.
(Claire Mawisa) Dr Thomas Funke heads the Sugarcane Growers’ Association, the voice of the industry since 1927.
(Thomas Funke) Sugarcane is a high bulk low weight product so in other words a sugar truck cannot drive a far distance with sugarcane its very limited to around 60km from the mill. Thereafter it just doesn’t make sense in terms of transport cost. So, a sugar mill has its cane suppliers surrounding it and from there it draws sugarcane to the mill.
(Claire Mawisa) The season begins in April when farmers deliver their cane to the mills to be crushed into sugar. It’s then sold and the income shared between mills and farmers. Each year, Tongaat Hulett buys more than a quarter of the country’s 18 million tonnes of sugar cane, much of it from small-scale farmers. But this year, no one knows if Tongaat’s mills will open. The company is 12 billion Rand in debt and might be liquidated. That would mean closing its doors after 134 years in business.
(Thomas Funke) Under liquidation, if its unfunded and the mills close, the doors close they don’t open again, the assets get mothballed while the liquidator fights for who gets the assets, I think that is the worst case scenario for us.
(Keval Bodasing) It’s a massive blow, if the mills don’t start on time this year, its gonna have a huge a huge impact on the rural economy of KZN. You know, we sustain many of the rural towns on the North Coast.
(Claire Mawisa) For more than a century, Tongaat Hullet has been buying land along KwaZulu-Natal’s North Coast, from KwaDukuza past Ballito and Umhlanga to Durban. Today it’s a corridor of continued multi-million Rand development, making it some of the most valuable land in the country. That makes land one of this sugar company’s most valuable assets. On communal land, small farmers grow cane on tiny plots, some as small as half a hectare. If Tongaat Hulett shifts its focus from sugar to land development, these farmers could be in serious trouble.
(Malusi Zondi) Hey
(Claire Mawisa) Hallo hallo, How are you?
(Malusi Zondi) How are you?
(Claire Mawisa) Very well thank you, good to meet you. Lets go.
(Malusi Zondi) The land has been protected historically by the monarchy. The land belongs to the Ngonyama trust, that’s how it is designated.
(Claire Mawisa) The Ingonyama Trust holds close to 3 million hectares of traditional land in KZN. Chancellor of the Zulu Royal House, iNkosi Malusi Zondi, says that land supports over 20 thousand small-scale farmers.
(Malusi Zondi) We’ve got reports that some already had faced strokes have faced heart attacks because they are worried how are they going to live with their families. Already there are no job opportunities in South Africa, government is trying, but when our people are crying to stand up, we are faced with this challenges.
(Claire Mawisa) By now, the mills should be almost ready for the season. But we’re told contractors have downed tools, unsure whether they’ll be paid.
(Thomas Funke) The mills are actually undergoing maintenance at the moment. So every day that is lost in repairing the mills means that the start-up date moves out by one day. So there is a critical bit of work that has to be done in order to get the mills ready for season start.
(Claire Mawisa) Time is ticking, but Tongaat Hulett couldn’t tell us whether the mills will open or not. Keval says farmers have been living in uncertainty for the past seven years. While some have given up, he’s hanging on.
(Keval Bodasing) I can't see myself doing anything other than cane farming. It's not like you can just switch to an alternate crop. We have really low potential soils for agriculture. So its not very easy to farm and then obviously the rolling hills pose quite a challenge. I’ve got the 6th generation that I’m preparing to take over after me and I am unsure whether they will actually have that opportunity.
(Thomas Funke) We found that there aren’t really any alternatives. Our farm sizes aren’t big enough for maize. Macadamias and avocados are options but extremely capital intensive. So the real solution for KZN is sugarcane. And what we need to try and focus on is diversification, so, alternative revenue streams, not only sugar and molasses.
(Claire Mawisa) Another option is for farmers to form co-operatives and build their own mills. This is one example: a brown sugar mill in the Midlands, founded and run by farmers for more than 100 years.
(Thomas Funke) When farmers are part of the milling operation and the value chain there’s that interest to make a success of the operations and perhaps that is the future.
(Claire Mawisa) But building a mill is expensive. Small farmers on communal land simply don’t have the resources to do it. Many are barely surviving on the cane they sell now, with some earning as little as R14 000 a season. And a visit to Durban’s harbour raises even more alarming questions for an industry already under severe pressure. This is a mountain of unrefined sugar waiting to leave the country, by law any sugar we can’t sell here locally must be exported, so this may look impressive but it’s not a situation we want to find ourselves in. That’s because our sugar is heaping up as imports have dominated the market.
(Kulani Siweya) For every tonne of sugar that is removed from the local producers by cheap imports, it place the livelihoods at risk.
(Claire Mawisa) Kulani Siweya monitors sugar imports and exports for the Sugar Association.
(Kulani Siweya) It has undercut our local producers to the tune of about 1.2 billion losses for the sector. And that 163 thousand tonnes is actually a 155% increase on imports that we have seen compared to the very same period in the last season.
(Claire Mawisa) It’s is also worrying to see so much sugar being exported as well, why is that?
(Kulani Siweya) For any sugar producer in the world, you get a better pricing in your local market then you would in the export market. And this is mainly driven because the big producers of sugar across the world, this is Brazil, India and Thailand, they produce sugar at a cost that is very very below the cost of production and essentially once they have met their demand they send their surplus sugar into the export market and by flooding that it does suppress and put pressure on the world prices so as soon as we then participate in the export market the sugar prices are really not the kind that will derive value for to realise any profits in this regard.
(Thomas Funke) So for every tonne that is imported, we lose arout seven and a half thousand Rand in revenue, which affects our jobs, our livelihoods. This money is essentially exported to support the Brazilian industry.
(Malusi Zondi) So, we are saying our government must also look into that so that our people can be able to sell also to sell where necessary. Sugar to me, is a treasurer of our people, its our mark. It’s history which you cannot remove that we have survived and we’ve made sure that we grow this and we are proud of it. Its our treasurer, we will always protect it.
(Claire Mawisa) Faced with mounting pressure, diversification appears to be the only solution. The aim is to transform mills into producing products like ethanol, a bio-fuel made from cane. It’s now a matter of survival for Keval Bodasing: the future of this land and its continued legacy now rest with him.
(Keval Bodasing) So, this is the gravesite of my grandfather Babu Bodasing and his wife.
(Claire Mawisa) Its quite remarkable that the land has stayed in the family.
(Keval Bodasing) Exactly, it’s a testament to the commitment and endurance of my forefathers and the fact that they managed to hold on to it for such a long time.
(Claire Mawisa) Does it weigh heavy on you that Babu’s legacy, everything that he’s built, might end with you?
(Keval Bodasing) Yes, it does. All the generations before us managed to hang on to the business and keep it going and you know, now we’re facing an uncertain future. So, it’s a sad story and an uncertain time for us and I would love for this to obviously continue and to make our mark in history.

Now, global competition and the collapse of a corporate giant threaten its future. As cheap imports replace local product and liquidation looms, farmers face the loss of an existence that’s been in their families for generations. Over a million livelihoods and decades of history hover on the brink as the industry faces a bitter reckoning. Producer: Anina Peens | Presenter: Claire Mawisa Script: SUGARCOATED COLLAPSE final for mnet (Keval Bodasing) Our story begins with my forefather, Babu Bodasing. He was born in Agra, Northern India and as we all know, Indians arrived in South Africa, in 1860.He boarded a ship on the first of August 1874. It was a month-long journey from Calcutta down to what was then Port Natal. And her arrived in South Africa, first of September 1874. He served his indentureship which was 5 years for the Glasgow natal sugar company where he was elevated to working at the sugar mill. (Claire Mawisa) Sugar cane was introduced in South Africa during British colonial rule in the 1800s. Thousands of workers were brought from India under indentureship, paid labour often likened to slavery. Conditions were harsh, with contracts binding workers to plantations for five to seven years. But after his contract finished, Keval Bodasing’s great, great grandfather chose to stay. (Keval Bodasing) He were given the option of a return passage back to India, or you could exchange that for a monetary value and he was able to use these proceeds to purchase 6 acres of land. By 1910 he had purchased this farm, which is known as Hydepark. He passed away in 1919 and at that time he had owned 8000 acres of land (Claire Mawisa) Wow (Keval Bodasing) And he became the largest landowner out of any of the Indentured labourers at the time. (Claire Mawisa) Was it always a desire as well for you to continue the legacy that is so rich? (Keval Bodasing) It was engrained in me from birth that I would one day continue the farming legacy that we have. And ah, so, I kind of knew this was my destiny no matter what happened. (Claire Mawisa) Vast stretches of sugarcane dominate the KwaZulu Natal coast. It’s been the lifeforce of the economy here for over a century. At the epicentre of what’s known as the sugar belt is the historic town of Tongaat. It’s the site of the Maidstone Mill, where the country’s first cane was processed in 1903. It was a vibrant and promising time. Companies like Tongaat Hulett gave farmers security, building an entire economy around the crop. (Keval Bodasing) One has to look at the canegrowers and the millers and how they are intertwined. Neither can exist without each other and the growers require milling capacity in order to sustain their business. This map is over a hundred years old (Claire Mawisa) The business model remained largely unchanged. Cane is still cut by hand, and generational growers like the Bodasings have generally delivered to the same mills. (Keval Bodasing) The N2 didn’t exist its currently on this alignment here. (Thomas Funke) As sugarcane is harvested, it has to be processed within 48 to 72 hours otherwise it deteriorates, and the farmers get penalised for sending poor quality cane to the sugar mill. (Claire Mawisa) Dr Thomas Funke heads the Sugarcane Growers’ Association, the voice of the industry since 1927. (Thomas Funke) Sugarcane is a high bulk low weight product so in other words a sugar truck cannot drive a far distance with sugarcane its very limited to around 60km from the mill. Thereafter it just doesn’t make sense in terms of transport cost. So, a sugar mill has its cane suppliers surrounding it and from there it draws sugarcane to the mill. (Claire Mawisa) The season begins in April when farmers deliver their cane to the mills to be crushed into sugar. It’s then sold and the income shared between mills and farmers. Each year, Tongaat Hulett buys more than a quarter of the country’s 18 million tonnes of sugar cane, much of it from small-scale farmers. But this year, no one knows if Tongaat’s mills will open. The company is 12 billion Rand in debt and might be liquidated. That would mean closing its doors after 134 years in business. (Thomas Funke) Under liquidation, if its unfunded and the mills close, the doors close they don’t open again, the assets get mothballed while the liquidator fights for who gets the assets, I think that is the worst case scenario for us. (Keval Bodasing) It’s a massive blow, if the mills don’t start on time this year, its gonna have a huge a huge impact on the rural economy of KZN. You know, we sustain many of the rural towns on the North Coast. (Claire Mawisa) For more than a century, Tongaat Hullet has been buying land along KwaZulu-Natal’s North Coast, from KwaDukuza past Ballito and Umhlanga to Durban. Today it’s a corridor of continued multi-million Rand development, making it some of the most valuable land in the country. That makes land one of this sugar company’s most valuable assets. On communal land, small farmers grow cane on tiny plots, some as small as half a hectare. If Tongaat Hulett shifts its focus from sugar to land development, these farmers could be in serious trouble. (Malusi Zondi) Hey (Claire Mawisa) Hallo hallo, How are you? (Malusi Zondi) How are you? (Claire Mawisa) Very well thank you, good to meet you. Lets go. (Malusi Zondi) The land has been protected historically by the monarchy. The land belongs to the Ngonyama trust, that’s how it is designated. (Claire Mawisa) The Ingonyama Trust holds close to 3 million hectares of traditional land in KZN. Chancellor of the Zulu Royal House, iNkosi Malusi Zondi, says that land supports over 20 thousand small-scale farmers. (Malusi Zondi) We’ve got reports that some already had faced strokes have faced heart attacks because they are worried how are they going to live with their families. Already there are no job opportunities in South Africa, government is trying, but when our people are crying to stand up, we are faced with this challenges. (Claire Mawisa) By now, the mills should be almost ready for the season. But we’re told contractors have downed tools, unsure whether they’ll be paid. (Thomas Funke) The mills are actually undergoing maintenance at the moment. So every day that is lost in repairing the mills means that the start-up date moves out by one day. So there is a critical bit of work that has to be done in order to get the mills ready for season start. (Claire Mawisa) Time is ticking, but Tongaat Hulett couldn’t tell us whether the mills will open or not. Keval says farmers have been living in uncertainty for the past seven years. While some have given up, he’s hanging on. (Keval Bodasing) I can't see myself doing anything other than cane farming. It's not like you can just switch to an alternate crop. We have really low potential soils for agriculture. So its not very easy to farm and then obviously the rolling hills pose quite a challenge. I’ve got the 6th generation that I’m preparing to take over after me and I am unsure whether they will actually have that opportunity. (Thomas Funke) We found that there aren’t really any alternatives. Our farm sizes aren’t big enough for maize. Macadamias and avocados are options but extremely capital intensive. So the real solution for KZN is sugarcane. And what we need to try and focus on is diversification, so, alternative revenue streams, not only sugar and molasses. (Claire Mawisa) Another option is for farmers to form co-operatives and build their own mills. This is one example: a brown sugar mill in the Midlands, founded and run by farmers for more than 100 years. (Thomas Funke) When farmers are part of the milling operation and the value chain there’s that interest to make a success of the operations and perhaps that is the future. (Claire Mawisa) But building a mill is expensive. Small farmers on communal land simply don’t have the resources to do it. Many are barely surviving on the cane they sell now, with some earning as little as R14 000 a season. And a visit to Durban’s harbour raises even more alarming questions for an industry already under severe pressure. This is a mountain of unrefined sugar waiting to leave the country, by law any sugar we can’t sell here locally must be exported, so this may look impressive but it’s not a situation we want to find ourselves in. That’s because our sugar is heaping up as imports have dominated the market. (Kulani Siweya) For every tonne of sugar that is removed from the local producers by cheap imports, it place the livelihoods at risk. (Claire Mawisa) Kulani Siweya monitors sugar imports and exports for the Sugar Association. (Kulani Siweya) It has undercut our local producers to the tune of about 1.2 billion losses for the sector. And that 163 thousand tonnes is actually a 155% increase on imports that we have seen compared to the very same period in the last season. (Claire Mawisa) It’s is also worrying to see so much sugar being exported as well, why is that? (Kulani Siweya) For any sugar producer in the world, you get a better pricing in your local market then you would in the export market. And this is mainly driven because the big producers of sugar across the world, this is Brazil, India and Thailand, they produce sugar at a cost that is very very below the cost of production and essentially once they have met their demand they send their surplus sugar into the export market and by flooding that it does suppress and put pressure on the world prices so as soon as we then participate in the export market the sugar prices are really not the kind that will derive value for to realise any profits in this regard. (Thomas Funke) So for every tonne that is imported, we lose arout seven and a half thousand Rand in revenue, which affects our jobs, our livelihoods. This money is essentially exported to support the Brazilian industry. (Malusi Zondi) So, we are saying our government must also look into that so that our people can be able to sell also to sell where necessary. Sugar to me, is a treasurer of our people, its our mark. It’s history which you cannot remove that we have survived and we’ve made sure that we grow this and we are proud of it. Its our treasurer, we will always protect it. (Claire Mawisa) Faced with mounting pressure, diversification appears to be the only solution. The aim is to transform mills into producing products like ethanol, a bio-fuel made from cane. It’s now a matter of survival for Keval Bodasing: the future of this land and its continued legacy now rest with him. (Keval Bodasing) So, this is the gravesite of my grandfather Babu Bodasing and his wife. (Claire Mawisa) Its quite remarkable that the land has stayed in the family. (Keval Bodasing) Exactly, it’s a testament to the commitment and endurance of my forefathers and the fact that they managed to hold on to it for such a long time. (Claire Mawisa) Does it weigh heavy on you that Babu’s legacy, everything that he’s built, might end with you? (Keval Bodasing) Yes, it does. All the generations before us managed to hang on to the business and keep it going and you know, now we’re facing an uncertain future. So, it’s a sad story and an uncertain time for us and I would love for this to obviously continue and to make our mark in history. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Along the north coast of KwaZulu-Natal, sugar built an empire over the past 130 years but now, its future no longer looks so sweet.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: This story captures the human cost of industrial collapse, following families whose lives span generations of sugar production, from indentured labour to modern land reform beneficiaries, now facing an uncertain future.
metadata.Summary: This is one of South Africa’s most important and underreported historical and economic stories, one that many younger generations may barely know. It began in 1860, when ships carrying indentured Indian labourers arrived on the shores of Durban to build what would become one of the country’s most influential agricultural industries. Over the decades, the sugar industry grew into a vast economic empire, shaping communities, sustaining generations of families, and controlling some of the most valuable land in South Africa. Entire towns were built around its mills, and its influence defined the development of KwaZulu-Natal’s north coast. Now, more than a century later, that empire faces an uncertain future, as corporate collapse, global competition, and a government widely criticised for failing to protect local industry, threaten to dismantle one of the country’s oldest economic foundations.
metadata.Further information: Tongaat Hulett is facing an almost certain liquidation. Its collapse threatens not only an industry, but entire towns, communities, and a history stretching back more than a century. Founded in 1892, Tongaat Hulett played a central role in the development of Durban’s north coast and the rise of the Indian middle class in KwaZulu-Natal. The company owns vast tracts of agricultural land, some of the most valuable in the country on the North Coast corridor between Ballito and Durban. It is this land that now sits at the centre of a growing dispute, leaving the future of hundreds of thousands of people uncertain. The company’s decline began in 2019, when it emerged that Tongaat Hulett had overstated its financial position by nearly R4 billion. It would become one of the biggest corporate scandals in South Africa since Steinhoff, yet received relatively little public scrutiny. Once listed on both the Johannesburg and London Stock Exchanges, the company was subsequently delisted from both, as investor confidence collapsed and banks withdrew their support. Crippled by debt, Tongaat Hulett entered business rescue in 2022. A Zimbabwean consortium, Vision Sugar, stepped in with the intention of rescuing the company. But disagreements between investors, creditors, and shareholders have stalled those efforts. Now, Tongaat Hulett is expected to file for liquidation on 24 February. Its bank accounts have already been frozen, and salaries will only be paid until the end of March. Beyond that, the future of its mills and the communities that depend on them, remains uncertain. The closure of a sugar mill is rarely temporary. Once shut down, the surrounding economic ecosystem begins to unravel. Farmers lose access to processing facilities. Workers lose employment. Local businesses collapse. Entire towns begin to decline. At the heart of the dispute is Tongaat Hulett’s land portfolio. Currently zoned for agriculture, parts of this land are valued at approximately R20,000 per hectare. But if rezoned for residential or industrial development, its value could increase exponentially, reaching as much as R10 million per hectare. With liquidation looming, this land will be sold to repay creditors. The fear among many is that it could ultimately fall into foreign hands, transforming one of South Africa’s most historically significant agricultural corridors into a development battleground. At the same time, the broader sugar industry is under mounting pressure from imported sugar. Cheap sugar from countries such as Brazil, India, and Thailand has flooded the South African market, increasing dramatically over the past year. Local farmers now find themselves unable to compete. Sugar is stockpiling in warehouses, unsold and unprocessed, while mills struggle to remain operational. The industry supports an intricate ecosystem that includes more than 20,000 small-scale farmers, many of whom are land reform beneficiaries. For these farmers, sugar is not just a crop, it is their only source of income. The collapse of Tongaat Hulett would trigger widespread unemployment, accelerate rural decline, and drive migration into already overcrowded cities. In KwaZulu-Natal, where economic instability has historically contributed to social unrest, the consequences could be severe. Tongaat Hulett’s history is deeply intertwined with South Africa’s past. From the 1860s, Indian labourers were brought to work on the sugar plantations. Many were housed in barracks built by the company. Sunrise Barracks remains one of the oldest surviving examples. Today, descendants of those original labourers still live there, their lives spanning generations of work in the sugar fields and mills. That history now stands on the edge of disappearance. There are growing concerns that the barracks may be demolished as part of future land redevelopment. What took generations to build could vanish within years. Entire towns, including Empangeni, Amatikulu, Mount Edgecombe, Maidstone, and communities as far as Pongola owe their existence to the sugar industry. The north coast itself was shaped by sugar. While development will inevitably continue, the question remains what will happen to the people whose lives, livelihoods, and identities are rooted in this land. The land will endure. The economy will move forward. But for those who built their lives around sugar, the future has never been more uncertain.
